AI.motivation: The nature and luminosity evolution of compact stellar systems (globular clusters, ultra-compact dwarfs) across cosmic time remain poorly constrained; high-redshift massive clusters offer a window to test whether observed brightening at earlier epochs reflects younger, more luminous stellar populations.
AI.method: Deep JWST/NIRCam imaging in F115W, F150W, and F200W of the massive cluster MACS J1149.5+2223 at z=0.544; photometric and morphological selection of unresolved compact sources; comparison of the observed luminosity distribution to an expected GCLF with adopted turnover m_0=33.66 mag (from Abell 2744 and MACS 0417); forward-modeled fitting of the bright-side slope; comparison with PARSEC simple stellar population models.
AI.result: 1,202 unresolved compact-source candidates identified. The luminosity distribution samples only the bright side of the GCLF, several magnitudes above turnover. Forward-modeled fit yields sigma=1.71 mag, characterizing the observed bright-side slope rather than the intrinsic GCLF width. Brightest sources reach luminosities comparable to ultra-compact dwarfs, though stellar-population degeneracies and possible foreground contamination prevent definitive classification. Elevated luminosities are consistent with expected fading of younger stellar populations.
AI.conclusion: MACS 1149 extends the emerging observational sequence of compact stellar systems across redshifts and supports stellar population fading as an important contributor to their luminosity evolution across cosmic time.

title: Zeeman-Doppler imaging of active young Suns. New surface magnetic field maps for BE Cet, HN Peg, and kappa1 Cet
summary: Studying the magnetic activity of young solar analogues is important for understanding the dynamo mechanisms of the Sun and other late-type stars. We aimed to determine the surface magnetic field topology of four stars, analogues to the young Sun. This will contribute to long-term studies of the evolution of magnetic activity on different timescales of these targets. We obtained high resolution spectropolarimetric measurements with the HARPSpol instrument mounted at the ESO 3.6m telescope in the epoch 2021.6, and the SOFIN instrument, mounted on the 2.56m NOT telescope in epochs 2017.4 and 2021.5. The signal-to-noise ratio of the observations was boosted with least squares deconvolution. The surface magnetic field maps were calculated with the Zeeman-Doppler imaging technique. The magnetic field is decomposed into spherical harmonic expansions, allowing us to quantify the contributions from the axisymmetric and non-axisymmetric components, as well as the poloidal and toroidal fields. Out of the four stars observed (BE Cet, HN Peg, kappa1 Cet, V1358 Ori), three (BE Cet, HN Peg, kappa1 Cet) show clear signs of magnetic fields. Only one star, BE Cet shows clear evidence for the dominance of non-axisymmetric modes and the poloidal field being more dominant than the toroidal. HN Peg also shows signs of a stronger poloidal than a toroidal field, indicating an α^2 dynamo, where the convective turbulence effects dominate over the differential rotation. The magnetic field of V1358 Ori could not be reliably reconstructed.

AI.tldr: Zeeman-Doppler imaging of four young solar analogues reveals detectable surface magnetic fields in three targets, with BE Cet showing dominant non-axisymmetric and poloidal fields, and HN Peg indicating an α² dynamo.
AI.motivation: Understanding the dynamo mechanisms operating in the Sun and other late-type stars requires studying the magnetic activity of young solar analogues, and long-term monitoring of such targets constrains the evolution of magnetic activity across different timescales.
AI.method: High-resolution spectropolarimetric observations were obtained with HARPSpol at the ESO 3.6 m telescope (epoch 2021.6) and SOFIN at the 2.56 m NOT telescope (epochs 2017.4 and 2021.5). S/N was enhanced via least-squares deconvolution, and surface magnetic field maps were reconstructed using Zeeman-Doppler imaging. The field was decomposed into spherical harmonic expansions to quantify axisymmetric versus non-axisymmetric and poloidal versus toroidal contributions.
AI.result: Of the four stars (BE Cet, HN Peg, kappa1 Cet, V1358 Ori), three (BE Cet, HN Peg, kappa1 Cet) show clear magnetic field signatures. BE Cet alone shows clear evidence for dominant non-axisymmetric modes and a poloidal field stronger than the toroidal component. HN Peg also shows a stronger poloidal than toroidal field, indicative of an α² dynamo in which convective turbulence effects dominate over differential rotation. The field of V1358 Ori could not be reliably reconstructed.
AI.conclusion: The surface magnetic topologies of three young solar analogues are characterized, with poloidal-dominated fields in BE Cet and HN Peg pointing to α² dynamo action; these results support continued long-term monitoring of magnetic activity evolution in young solar-type stars.

title: Model-Driven Stellar Spectroscopy with the Total Differential Spectral Model (TDSM): Framework and Its Application to 11 Million LAMOST Low-Resolution Spectra
summary: Deriving stellar astrophysical parameters from large-scale spectroscopic surveys requires accurate modeling of spectra across a wide wavelength coverage and a broad range of stellar parameter space, which remains a great challenge. In this work, we present \texttt{TDSM}, a physically motivated neural network architecture that self-consistently emulates both the flux and its first-order derivative of the ab initio stellar spectra. The method enables accurate and precise emulation of Kurucz synthetic spectra with severely blended features at $R \simeq 2000$ in a high-dimensional parameter space, achieving a typical pixel-wise flux precision of 0.05\% in the wavelength range $3700<λ<9000$Å over the parameter range of $3000 < T_{\rm eff} < 45,000$~K, $-1 < \log g < 5$, and $-4.0 < \mathrm{[Fe/H]} < 0.5$. The model is applied to LAMOST DR10 to derive stellar parameters for 11 million spectra spanning the full model parameter range. We conduct detailed refinement and calibration efforts to mitigate systematic errors, which are revealed to be significant and complex due to imperfections in the ab initio model atmosphere. The resultant catalog provides eight stellar labels -- $T_{\rm eff}$, $\log g$, $v_{\rm mic}$, [Fe/H], [$α$/Fe], [C/Fe], [N/Fe], and [Mg/Fe] -- for 8 million unique stars (11 million spectra including repeat observations) across the full parameter space. This adds a valuable dataset for studies of Galactic structure and archaeology, stellar populations, and related areas of astrophysics.

AI.tldr: TDSM is a physically motivated neural network that jointly emulates stellar spectral flux and its first-order derivative, achieving 0.05% per-pixel accuracy on Kurucz spectra at R≃2000 and enabling stellar-label derivation for 11 million LAMOST DR10 spectra.
AI.motivation: Deriving stellar astrophysical parameters from large spectroscopic surveys demands accurate spectral modeling over broad wavelength coverage and wide stellar parameter space, which is a major challenge. Existing emulation approaches struggle with severely blended features in high-dimensional parameter space and with systematic errors from ab initio model atmosphere imperfections.
AI.method: A physically motivated neural network architecture (TDSM) that self-consistently emulates both the flux and its first-order derivative of ab initio stellar spectra. Trained on Kurucz synthetic spectra at R≃2000 over 3000<Teff<45,000 K, -1<log g<5, -4.0<[Fe/H]<0.5, and 3700-9000 Å. Applied to LAMOST DR10 with detailed refinement and calibration to mitigate systematic errors.
AI.result: Achieves typical pixel-wise flux precision of 0.05% in 3700-9000 Å across the full parameter range. The model derives eight labels (Teff, log g, v_mic, [Fe/H], [α/Fe], [C/Fe], [N/Fe], [Mg/Fe]) for 8 million unique stars (11 million spectra) spanning the full parameter space. Systematic errors are revealed to be significant and complex due to ab initio model atmosphere imperfections.
AI.conclusion: The TDSM self-consistent flux-and-derivative emulation delivers high-precision spectral modeling, and the resulting large catalog of stellar labels provides a valuable dataset for studies of Galactic structure and archaeology, stellar populations, and related astrophysics.

title: Geometric tracking of a halo CME using full-circle wide-field views from PUNCH
summary: We tracked the large, geoeffective halo coronal mass ejection (CME) of 2025-May-31 across the very wide field of view of the Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) mission, as a proof of concept for data-informed forecasting of CME arrival times at Earth. using simple point-and-click measurement of the front location as far as 47 degrees away from the Sun itself, we constrained an analytic "ludicrous ice-cream cone" geometric model with just three parameters: position angle, off-Earth-Sun angle, and propagation speed. We show that the model is sufficient to capture the bulk envelope of the CME, and also insufficient to capture the complexity of the CME's evolution. We generated simulated arrival-time forecasts for the CME by extrapolating the constant-velocity propagation to determine the time of impact with Earth. These "retro-forecasts" converged to within 30 +/- 15 minutes of the actual arrival time, 8 hours prior to arrival. The convergence was marked by a clear inflection point in the curve of predicted-arrival-time vs time-of-forecast. We conclude that continuous wide-field tracking is sufficiently powerful to enable even crude models to substantially improve arrival-time forecasting precision, and discuss future work required both to validate this single-event result and to extend it to more sophisticated analyses.

AI.tldr: Using PUNCH's wide field of view, the authors track the 2025-May-31 halo CME out to 47° from the Sun and constrain a 3-parameter "ludicrous ice-cream cone" geometric model to produce retro-forecasts that converged to within 30 ± 15 minutes of the actual Earth arrival time, 8 hours before impact.
AI.motivation: Data-informed forecasting of CME arrival times at Earth remains imprecise; the authors test whether continuous wide-field tracking from PUNCH can enable even simple models to substantially improve arrival-time precision.
AI.method: Point-and-click measurement of the CME front location (up to 47° from the Sun) constrains an analytic "ludicrous ice-cream cone" geometric model with three parameters: position angle, off-Earth-Sun angle, and propagation speed. Constant-velocity extrapolation yields simulated arrival-time "retro-forecasts."
AI.result: The model captures the bulk CME envelope but not the full complexity of its evolution. Retro-forecasts converged to within 30 ± 15 minutes of the actual arrival time 8 hours prior, marked by a clear inflection point in predicted-arrival-time vs. time-of-forecast.
AI.conclusion: Continuous wide-field tracking is powerful enough to let even crude models substantially improve arrival-time forecasting precision; future work is needed to validate this single-event result and extend it to more sophisticated analyses.

title: LAMOST III Low-resolution Spectroscopic Survey: Overview and Target Selection
comment: 24 pages, 14 figures, 2 tables. Accepted by SCIENCE CHINA: Physics, Mechanics & Astronomy
summary: We present an overview of the LAMOST III Low-resolution Spectroscopic Survey (LRS), including its scientific goals, target selection strategy, and current observing status. Targets in the main survey are selected via weighted random sampling, using the inverse local density in the Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram and in the G-magnitude distribution, with additional enhancement in selected regions of the HR diagram. The main survey is complemented by 35 dedicated add-on catalogs (including very metal-poor star candidates, halo stars, hot/young stars, wide binaries, extragalactic sources and so on) and a time-domain program providing multi-epoch spectroscopy of binaries and other peculiar systems. LAMOST III LRS is designed to map the structure and evolution of the Galactic disk, reconstruct the assembly and early chemical-enrichment history of the Galactic halo, improve stellar-parameter calibration, and characterize rare and variable objects. By June 2025, the LAMOST III LRS had obtained 1.53 million low-resolution spectra from 658 plates, corresponding to 1,264,052 unique sources. Relative to LAMOST I+II, the current sample is enriched in O/B stars, subgiants, main-sequence turn-off stars, metal-poor stars, and other previously underrepresented populations. In particular, the fractions of metal-poor and very metal-poor stars increase from 3.8% and 0.4% in LAMOST I+II to 9.0% and 1.1% in LAMOST III LRS, respectively, demonstrating the improved efficiency of the revised target-selection strategy for Galactic archaeology and stellar astrophysics.

AI.tldr: Overview of the LAMOST III low-resolution spectroscopic survey, whose weighted-random target selection in the HR diagram and G-magnitude space yields a sample strongly enriched in O/B stars, turn-off stars, and metal-poor stars relative to LAMOST I+II.
AI.motivation: LAMOST I+II samples underrepresented key populations (O/B stars, subgiants, main-sequence turn-off stars, metal-poor stars), limiting studies of Galactic disk/halo structure, early chemical enrichment, and stellar-parameter calibration; a revised selection strategy is needed to improve sampling efficiency for Galactic archaeology and stellar astrophysics.
AI.method: Weighted random sampling of main-survey targets using inverse local density in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and in the G-magnitude distribution, with enhancement in selected HR-diagram regions; complemented by 35 add-on catalogs (very metal-poor candidates, halo stars, hot/young stars, wide binaries, extragalactic sources, etc.) and a time-domain program for multi-epoch spectroscopy of binaries and peculiar systems.
AI.result: By June 2025, 1.53 million low-resolution spectra from 658 plates were obtained, corresponding to 1,264,052 unique sources. The sample is enriched in O/B stars, subgiants, main-sequence turn-off stars, and metal-poor stars; metal-poor and very metal-poor fractions rise from 3.8% and 0.4% (LAMOST I+II) to 9.0% and 1.1% (LAMOST III), respectively.
AI.conclusion: The revised target-selection strategy substantially improves sampling efficiency for previously underrepresented populations, demonstrating its effectiveness for Galactic archaeology and stellar astrophysics and positioning LAMOST III LRS to map Galactic disk structure/evolution and reconstruct the halo's assembly and early chemical-enrichment history.

title: Ca II IRT activity indices from $Gaia$ spectroscopy: a baseline method for photospheric contribution estimates
comment: 14 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: The $Gaia$ high-resolution spectroscopic observations using Radial Velocity Spectrometer offers a unique opportunity to study stellar Ca II infrared triplet (IRT) activity. A key step in estimating activity indices is subtracting the photospheric contribution. The canonical template-based method often fails because, for many stars, the observed line cores are deeper than the model predictions, which prevents valid activity measurements. In this work, we explore an alternative approach that constructs a baseline from less active stars as a function of effective temperature (and metallicity) to represent the photospheric contribution. Our results show that, for dwarf stars, compared with the canonical method, the baseline method not only yields far more objects with valid activity measurements, but also avoids many extremely low and unreliable values (e.g., log$R'_{\rm IRT} \lesssim -6$). The Ca II IRT activity indices derived from the baseline method correlate well with other activity proxies, confirming their reliability as activity indicators. Furthermore, they show a relation with stellar rotation, not only recovering the typical rotation--activity relation, but also revealing fine structures that may be associated with different regimes in gyrochronology. Our findings suggest that the baseline method can serve as a robust alternative for deriving accurate activity estimates, and will be particularly useful for obtaining activity indices for tens of millions of stars with the upcoming $Gaia$ Data Release 4.

AI.tldr: A baseline method using less active stars as a function of Teff (and metallicity) offers a robust alternative to template-based subtraction for deriving Ca II IRT activity indices from Gaia RVS spectra, dramatically increasing valid measurements and revealing rotation-activity fine structure.
AI.motivation: Estimating stellar Ca II infrared triplet (IRT) activity from Gaia Radial Velocity Spectrometer spectra requires removing the photospheric contribution. The canonical template-based method often fails because observed line cores are frequently deeper than model predictions, preventing valid activity measurements.
AI.method: Construct a photospheric baseline from less active stars as a function of effective temperature (and metallicity) instead of relying on model templates, and compare the resulting activity indices with the canonical template-based approach.
AI.result: For dwarf stars, the baseline method yields far more objects with valid activity measurements than the canonical method and avoids many extremely low, unreliable values (e.g., log R'IRT ≲ -6). The derived Ca II IRT indices correlate well with other activity proxies and show a relation with stellar rotation, recovering the standard rotation-activity relation while revealing fine structures possibly linked to different gyrochronology regimes.
AI.conclusion: The baseline method is a robust alternative for accurate activity estimation and will be particularly useful for obtaining activity indices for tens of millions of stars in the upcoming Gaia Data Release 4.

title: Orbital decomposition and evolution of LEGA-C-like galaxies in IllustrisTNG from z = 1 to z = 0
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A on 27/10/2026
summary: Stellar orbits encode the dynamical history of galaxies and provide a physically motivated link between galaxy structures and assembly processes. Although orbit-based decompositions are well established in the Local Universe, their evolution across cosmic time, especially at higher redshifts, remains poorly explored. We investigate the orbital structure of \texttt{LEGA-C-like} galaxies in the \texttt{TNG100} simulation from $z=1$ to $z=0$ to identify how stellar mass, star formation activity, environment, merger history, gas content, and ex situ stellar mass growth shape their orbital transformation. We decomposed the stellar orbital structure of simulated galaxies into cold, warm, hot, and counter-rotating (CR) components using time-averaged orbital circularities. We find a strong mass dependence of orbital structure at $z=0$ as well as at $z=1$. Galaxies below $\log(M_\star/M_\odot)\sim11.2$ have a combined warm and cold orbital fraction of $\sim70\%$, whereas more massive systems have a hot-orbit fraction of $\sim60\%$. These trends are consistent with assembly pathways driven predominantly by wet and dry major mergers, respectively. Tracking the same galaxies to $z=0$ reveals a systematic, but mass-dependent, evolution toward lower rotational support: At both low and high stellar masses, the hot-orbit fraction increases, whereas the relative change is greater in low-mass galaxies. The survival of cold structure depends strongly on the star formation state at $z=1$; star-forming progenitors retain substantially larger cold fractions than the quiescent progenitors. At both redshifts, the orbital fractions show a rise (decline) in hot and CR (cold and warm) orbits with the ex situ stellar mass fraction at a fixed stellar mass. These results provide the first evolutionary framework for interpreting orbit-based decompositions of galaxies at the \texttt{LEGA-C} epoch.

AI.tldr: Using TNG100 simulations, the authors decompose LEGA-C-like galaxies into cold, warm, hot, and counter-rotating orbit components from z=1 to z=0, finding strong mass-dependent orbital structure and a systematic evolution toward lower rotational support, with survival of cold structure tied to star formation state and ex situ mass fraction.
AI.motivation: Orbit-based decompositions link galaxy structure to assembly history and are well established in the Local Universe, but how orbital structure evolves across cosmic time (especially at higher redshift, e.g. the LEGA-C epoch) remains poorly explored.
AI.method: Decomposed the stellar orbital structure of LEGA-C-like galaxies in TNG100 from z=1 to z=0 into cold, warm, hot, and counter-rotating (CR) components using time-averaged orbital circularities, then related orbital fractions to stellar mass, star formation activity, environment, merger history, gas content, and ex situ stellar mass fraction.
AI.result: Strong mass dependence of orbital structure at both z=0 and z=1: galaxies below log(M*/Msun)~11.2 have ~70% combined warm+cold fraction, while more massive systems have ~60% hot-orbit fraction, consistent with wet vs. dry major-merger assembly. Tracking galaxies to z=0 shows mass-dependent evolution toward lower rotational support (hot fraction rises at all masses, more strongly in low-mass systems). Cold-structure survival depends on z=1 star formation state (star-forming progenitors retain larger cold fractions). At fixed mass, hot and CR fractions rise while cold and warm fractions decline with increasing ex situ stellar mass fraction.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the first evolutionary framework for interpreting orbit-based decompositions of galaxies at the LEGA-C epoch, showing that orbital structure is shaped by mass-dependent assembly pathways and modulated by star formation state and ex situ mass growth.

title: XRISM/Xtend detection of solar wind charge exchange induced by multiple coronal mass ejections in 2024 August
comment: 11 pages, 12 figures, 2 tables; published online in PASJ; scheduled for publication in Vol. 78, Issue 6
summary: Solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) emission is often a major component of the soft X-ray background, but it also provides a remote diagnostic of the composition and ionization state of solar wind plasma. We present an analysis of a SWCX event observed with XRISM/Xtend during 2024 August 9-13. The event occurred during intense solar activity with multiple flares, including an X1.3-class solar flare, and associated coronal mass ejections (CMEs). We found a clear enhancement in the 0.3-3.0 keV count rate that occurred nearly simultaneously with an increase in the solar wind proton flux measured by ACE. We fitted the spectrum during the enhancement period with a set of Gaussian emission lines. In addition to the commonly detected C, N, and O lines, we detected Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe lines at $>15σ$ significance. We extracted two characteristic periods within the enhanced interval based on the CME arrival timeline. The O$_{\rm VIII}$/Si$_{\rm XIII}$ line ratio changed significantly between the two periods, suggesting contributions from multiple CME components. We then applied the AtomDB charge exchange model with a multi-temperature setup. The estimated ionization temperatures for Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe increased with the peak soft X-ray flux of the associated solar flares. This trend suggests that coronal heating becomes more efficient for more intense flares. Meanwhile, the ionization temperatures were lower than typical flare electron temperatures, implying that CME plasma may have been released into interplanetary space under non-equilibrium ionization conditions. We also found an indication of an inverse-FIP pattern, with reduced relative abundances of Si and S. These results demonstrate that XRISM/Xtend can diagnose the coronal plasma through SWCX emission, including heavy ions such as Ne, Mg, and Si, which are difficult to measure with current in-situ instruments (e.g., ACE satellite).

AI.tldr: XRISM/Xtend observed a solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) event during the intense solar activity of 2024 August 9–13, detecting C, N, O, Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe emission lines and using them to diagnose CME plasma composition and ionization state.
AI.motivation: SWCX emission is a major contributor to the soft X-ray background and offers a remote probe of solar wind composition and ionization, yet heavy ions like Ne, Mg, and Si are hard to measure with in-situ instruments such as ACE, motivating high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy.
AI.method: Analysis of an XRISM/Xtend observation of a SWCX event coincident with flares (including X1.3) and CMEs. The enhancement spectrum (0.3–3.0 keV) was fit with Gaussian emission lines; two sub-periods were defined from the CME arrival timeline and compared via the O VIII/Si XIII ratio. An AtomDB charge exchange model with multi-temperature setup was applied to estimate ionization temperatures.
AI.result: A clear count-rate enhancement coincided with an ACE proton-flux increase. Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe lines were detected at >15σ. The O VIII/Si XIII ratio changed significantly between the two periods, indicating multiple CME components. Ionization temperatures of Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe rose with peak flare soft X-ray flux but remained below typical flare electron temperatures. An inverse-FIP pattern was indicated by reduced Si and S abundances.
AI.conclusion: Coronal heating appears more efficient for more intense flares; CME plasma may be released with non-equilibrium ionization. XRISM/Xtend can diagnose coronal plasma via SWCX emission, including heavy ions inaccessible to current in-situ instruments.

title: The LAMOST Galaxy Parameter Catalog (LAGC): Stellar Populations, Kinematics, and Emission Lines of Galaxies in the LAMOST Spectroscopic Survey
summary: The LAMOST Galaxy Parameter Catalog (LAGC) is a value-added data product of the LAMOST spectroscopic survey, generated by an automated spectral-fitting pipeline and released as a continuously updated catalogue series. Despite the vast data volume of the LAMOST spectroscopic survey, no dedicated, homogeneous pipeline had previously been able to extract stellar population, kinematic, and emission-line information simultaneously from its galaxy spectra, primarily because of the poorly controlled absolute flux calibration and a line spread function (LSF) that varies with wavelength, fibre, and time. The pipeline addresses both challenges through the SEW full-spectrum fitting method, which operates in equivalent-width space and is therefore immune to multiplicative flux-calibration errors, together with an accurate, wavelength-dependent model of the LAMOST LSF that enables unbiased kinematic measurements. As the pilot release of the catalogue series, we process the full galaxy sample of the latest LAMOST data release (283,691 spectra) and measure stellar population parameters, stellar and gas kinematics, and equivalent widths of 19 emission lines, each with bootstrap-based uncertainties. Repeat LAMOST observations confirm that the measurements are reproducible and that the bootstrap uncertainties are well calibrated, while comparison with SDSS shows only minor systematic offsets, attributable mainly to the SDSS LSF modelling. The measurements reproduce the well-established relations of the local galaxy population, and the catalogue will be publicly available and continuously updated as new observations become available. LAGC thus provides a reliable scientific catalogue for galaxy evolution studies, while the methodology behind it offers a blueprint for the next generation of fibre-fed spectroscopic surveys.

AI.tldr: LAGC is a value-added catalogue from the LAMOST survey that measures stellar populations, kinematics, and emission lines for 283,691 galaxy spectra using the SEW equivalent-width-space fitting method plus an accurate wavelength-dependent LSF model, with validated bootstrap uncertainties.
AI.motivation: No homogeneous pipeline could previously extract stellar population, kinematic, and emission-line information simultaneously from LAMOST galaxy spectra, mainly due to poorly controlled absolute flux calibration and a line spread function (LSF) varying with wavelength, fibre, and time.
AI.method: SEW full-spectrum fitting in equivalent-width space (immune to multiplicative flux-calibration errors) combined with an accurate wavelength-dependent LAMOST LSF model for unbiased kinematics; applied to the full galaxy sample of the latest LAMOST data release.
AI.result: Processed 283,691 galaxy spectra, measuring stellar population parameters, stellar and gas kinematics, and equivalent widths of 19 emission lines, each with bootstrap uncertainties. Repeat observations confirm reproducibility and well-calibrated errors; SDSS comparison shows only minor systematic offsets (attributed to SDSS LSF modelling); measurements reproduce known relations of the local galaxy population.
AI.conclusion: LAGC provides a reliable scientific catalogue for galaxy evolution studies, to be publicly released and continuously updated, and its methodology offers a blueprint for the next generation of fibre-fed spectroscopic surveys.

title: Simulating high-speed solar wind streams from coronal holes using an L5-L1 configuration of Lagrangian points
summary: Coronal holes (CHs) are known to be sources of high-speed solar wind streams (HSSs), yet the physical mechanisms linking CH position and characteristics to solar wind (SW) behaviour remain unclear. Our results reveal that the latitude of CHs, especially smaller ones, combined with the heliographic latitude of the solar disk's central point (B0 angle), plays a critical role in driving discrepancies in SW velocity across the heliosphere. To investigate this, we use archival data from STEREO-B, STEREO-A, and Earth to simulate an L5-L1 configuration, where L5 is a vantage point approximately behind Earth in its orbit (as proposed for the Vigil mission), and L1 is between Earth and the Sun where SW measurements are typically taken. We use these insights to develop a predictive algorithm for HSSs, beginning with an analysis of the separation angle and distances between L5 and L1. We then introduce a predictive indicator and empirical criteria based on CH properties and the B0 angle to adjust for changes in SW velocity at L1. Our results show that the L5 viewpoint demonstrates the capability to significantly improve the accuracy and lead times of HSS predictions, enhancing our understanding of the CH-HSS relationship and potentially improving space weather forecasting.

AI.tldr: Solar coronal hole latitude (especially for small CHs) and the B0 angle drive discrepancies in solar wind velocity between L5 and L1; an L5 vantage point improves high-speed stream prediction accuracy and lead time.
AI.motivation: Coronal holes (CHs) are sources of high-speed solar wind streams (HSSs), but the physical link between CH position/characteristics and solar wind behavior—particularly how velocity differs across vantage points—remains unclear. This limits both physical understanding and forecasting skill.
AI.method: Using archival data from STEREO-B, STEREO-A, and Earth, the authors emulate an L5–L1 configuration (L5 as a vantage point behind Earth, as proposed for Vigil; L1 as the typical measurement point). They analyze the separation angle and distances between L5 and L1, then derive a predictive indicator and empirical criteria based on CH properties and the B0 angle to adjust solar wind velocity expected at L1, forming an HSS prediction algorithm.
AI.result: CH latitude—especially for smaller CHs—together with the B0 angle plays a critical role in explaining discrepancies in solar wind velocity across the heliosphere. The L5 viewpoint significantly improves both the accuracy and lead times of HSS predictions.
AI.conclusion: The findings clarify the CH–HSS relationship and demonstrate that L5 observations can enhance HSS forecasting, with potential benefits for operational space weather prediction.

title: Gravitational Potential of CALIFA Galaxies from the Blue Cloud to the Red Sequence
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 1 Table; submitted to Proceedings of the XV Bulgarian-Serbian Astronomical Conference (Varna, Sept 13-18, 2026); Publ. Astron. Soc. "Rudjer Boskovic"
summary: We explore the gravitational potential of 238 (E1$-$Sdm) CALIFA galaxies from the Blue cloud to the Red Sequence using the star formation rate$-$stellar mass diagram ($\mathrm{SFR}-M_\star$) diagnosis. On average, galaxies in the Blue cloud possess slow-rising circular velocity curves (CVCs), those in the Green valley have flat CVCs, while galaxies in the Red sequence are characterised with peaked CVCs. Both the maximum circular velocity ($V_{c,\mathrm{max}}$) and asymptotic circular velocity ($V_{c,\mathrm{flat}}$) of the galaxies increase from the Blue cloud to the Red sequence, and show approximately linear relations with the logarithmic offsets from the star-forming main sequence ($Δ\mathrm{SFR}$s). The $Δ\mathrm{SFR}-\log_{10}(V_{c,\mathrm{max}})$ relation has a steeper slope ($-0.154 \pm 0.012$) than the $Δ\mathrm{SFR}-\log_{10}(V_{c,\mathrm{flat}})$ relation ($-0.124 \pm 0.011$). These results suggest that $V_{c,\mathrm{max}}$, tracing the inner gravitational potential, indicates a stronger variation along the quenching parameter $Δ\mathrm{SFR}$ than $V_{c,\mathrm{flat}}$, which is more strongly influenced by the outer mass distribution and dark matter halo.

AI.tldr: Using 238 CALIFA galaxies, the paper finds that circular velocity curve (CVC) shapes and amplitudes vary systematically from the Blue cloud to the Red Sequence, with V_c,max responding more strongly than V_c,flat to the quenching parameter ΔSFR.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to connect galaxy gravitational potentials (traced by circular velocity curves) to their star formation state along the SFR–M⋆ diagram, testing how the inner versus outer mass distribution relates to quenching.
AI.method: The authors analyze the gravitational potentials of 238 (E1–Sdm) CALIFA galaxies, classifying them into the Blue cloud, Green valley, and Red Sequence via the SFR–M⋆ diagnostic and characterizing their CVCs. They measure V_c,max and V_c,flat and correlate these with ΔSFR, the logarithmic offset from the star-forming main sequence.
AI.result: Blue-cloud galaxies show slow-rising CVCs, Green-valley galaxies flat CVCs, and Red-Sequence galaxies peaked CVCs. Both V_c,max and V_c,flat increase from Blue cloud to Red Sequence and scale roughly linearly with ΔSFR. The ΔSFR–log(V_c,max) relation is steeper (−0.154 ± 0.012) than the ΔSFR–log(V_c,flat) relation (−0.124 ± 0.011).
AI.conclusion: V_c,max, probing the inner gravitational potential, varies more strongly with the quenching parameter ΔSFR than V_c,flat, which is more influenced by the outer mass distribution and dark matter halo. This indicates that the inner potential is more tightly linked to quenching than the outer potential.

title: Rotating Polytropic Twins and the Fragmentation Problem
summary: Polytropic n=1 stellar configurations with strong differential rotation have been considered. The so-called twin configurations: stars having almost identical integral characteristics, but clearly structurally different have been found. Hydrodynamic 3D modeling has been performed for two such structures and has shown that these configurations also differ in the dynamic aspect: one of them remains practically stationary, while the other turns out to be unstable with respect to the development of the bar mode and fragmentation. The gravitational wave signal accompanying the fragmentation process has been calculated.

AI.tldr: Polytropic n=1 differentially rotating stellar models exhibit "twin" configurations with nearly identical global quantities but distinct structures; 3D hydrodynamics shows one is stable/stationary while the other is bar-mode unstable and fragments, producing a computable gravitational-wave signal.
AI.motivation: To determine whether stars with nearly identical integral characteristics (twin configurations) can nevertheless differ dynamically, and to connect structural degeneracy of differentially rotating polytropes to stability and gravitational-wave emission.
AI.method: Construction of polytropic n=1 equilibrium models with strong differential rotation, identification of twin configurations sharing almost identical integral parameters but structurally different. Full 3D hydrodynamic simulations of two such structures, stability analysis with respect to the bar (m=2) mode, and computation of the gravitational-wave signal from the fragmentation process.
AI.result: The two twin configurations differ dynamically despite matching integral characteristics: one remains essentially stationary, whereas the other is unstable to bar-mode growth and fragments. The gravitational-wave signal accompanying fragmentation is calculated.
AI.conclusion: Integral (global) parameters are insufficient to determine the dynamical fate of strongly differentially rotating stars; structurally distinct twins can have divergent stability behavior, and the unstable branch yields a detectable fragmentation-driven gravitational-wave signature.

title: The Interplay of Stellar Feedback and Gravity in the Wat01-S208 Star-forming Complex
summary: To investigate the processes governing clustered star formation, we present a multi-wavelength study of the star-forming complex hosting clusters Waterloo 01 and [BDS2003]64 in Sh 2-208. Both clusters exhibit elongated morphologies, with radii of $\sim1.5$ and $\sim0.9$ pc, respectively, and are located at a common distance of $\sim3.5$ kpc. Wat01 displays hierarchical structure ($Q=0.6$) and signature of mass segregation ($Γ_{\rm MSR}=1.5\pm0.6$). Its relaxation time, comparable to or longer than its age, suggests that the observed segregation may have a primordial contribution. The mass function follows a single power law, $Γ=-1.62\pm0.15$, over $\sim0.7$-$19.6$ M$_\odot$. Molecular-line observations reveal distinct velocity components associated with S208 and Wat01, indicating different molecular environments within the complex. Wat01 is strongly shaped by massive-star feedback, with an evacuated cavity, surrounding shell, and compressed globules consistent with an expanding H\,{\sc ii} region; feedback may have promoted localized star formation, although a direct causal connection cannot be established. In contrast, \textit{Herschel} data uncover a hub-filament system (HFS) in S208, with the central hub associated with BDS64 and the H\,{\sc ii} region powered by 'S1'. The filaments remain relatively well-preserved, indicating that gravity continues to play an important role in assembling dense gas toward the hub and in clustered star formation, even as feedback begins to affect the immediate surroundings. Overall, this complex illustrates the coexistence of feedback-processed and comparatively less-disrupted star-forming environments, highlighting the evolving interplay between stellar feedback and gravity in clustered star formation.

AI.tldr: Multi-wavelength study of Sh 2-208 (clusters Waterloo 01 and [BDS2003]64) reveals two coexisting clustered star-formation modes: one dominated by massive-star feedback and one where gravity-driven hub-filament accretion still prevails.
AI.motivation: Clustered star formation is governed by the interplay of gravity and stellar feedback, but how these processes act within a single star-forming complex is poorly constrained. The authors target Sh 2-208, which hosts two embedded clusters (Wat01 and BDS64), to examine these processes in a common environment.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength analysis combining cluster structural characterization (elongated morphologies, Q parameter, mass segregation ratio Γ_MSR, relaxation time, mass function), molecular-line observations (velocity components), and Herschel far-IR data to map the dust/gas structure and H II regions.
AI.result: Both clusters are elongated (radii ~1.5 and ~0.9 pc) at a common distance of ~3.5 kpc. Wat01 shows hierarchical structure (Q=0.6) and mass segregation (Γ_MSR=1.5±0.6) whose relaxation time is comparable to or longer than its age, implying a possible primordial origin; its mass function is a single power law, Γ=-1.62±0.15 (0.7–19.6 M_sun). Molecular lines show distinct velocity components for S208 and Wat01. Wat01 is strongly shaped by massive-star feedback (evacuated cavity, shell, compressed globules, expanding H II region). Herschel data reveal a hub-filament system in S208 with the hub at BDS64 and an H II region powered by 'S1'; filaments remain well-preserved.
AI.conclusion: Sh 2-208 illustrates the coexistence of a feedback-processed environment (Wat01) and a comparatively less-disrupted, gravity-dominated hub-filament environment (BDS64/S208), highlighting the evolving balance between stellar feedback and gravity in clustered star formation.

title: Mapping the obscured Galactic disk: ERIS J-band low-resolution spectroscopy of 27 Classical Cepheids
comment: Paper accepted for publication in the section "5. Galactic structure, stellar clusters and populations" of Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Classical Cepheids (CCs) are standard candles and key tracers of young stellar populations. However, their use in the most obscured regions is hampered by the high interstellar extinction at optical wavelengths. Near-infrared spectroscopy offers major advantages by greatly reducing absorption corrections and enabling access to regions of the Milky Way that are still poorly sampled. In this work, we determine the atmospheric parameters and abundances of Fe, Mg and Si for a sample of 27 CCs based on observations with ERIS@VLT in J-band low-resolution mode ($R \sim 4000$). Combining PySME with 1D MARCS atmosphere models and non local thermal equilibrium grids, we simultaneous optimise the atmospheric parameters through spectral fitting. This method is validated with a direct comparison with high-resolution optical investigations and re-analysis of archive optical spectra for the targets in common. The results show good consistency in both metallicity and chemical abundances. We obtain mean abundance ratios of $\mathrm{\langle[Mg/Fe]\rangle=0.01\pm0.12~dex}$ and $\mathrm{\langle[Si/Fe]\rangle=0.10\pm0.09~dex}$, in agreement with reference samples. Moreover, we provide for the first time the Mg and Si abundances of 12 CCs. Finally, we have found distinct kinematic properties for two of the most distant Galactic CCs, located at Galactocentric distances of $\mathrm{\approx 28-29~kpc}$ and with extreme values of vertical height, $\mathrm{\approx +4.8~kpc}$ and $\mathrm{\approx -5.3~kpc}$; more data are required to constrain their nature. Our results confirm that J-band spectroscopy at low-resolution can be used as a good diagnostic for the chemical investigation in highly obscured Galactic regions, otherwise inaccessible at optical wavelengths.

AI.tldr: J-band low-resolution (R~4000) ERIS@VLT spectroscopy combined with PySME, 1D MARCS models and NLTE grids yields consistent atmospheric parameters and Fe, Mg, Si abundances for 27 classical Cepheids, establishing J-band spectroscopy as a viable diagnostic in highly obscured Galactic regions.
AI.motivation: Classical Cepheids are key standard candles and tracers of young stellar populations, but their utility in the most obscured regions is limited by high interstellar extinction at optical wavelengths. Near-infrared spectroscopy reduces absorption corrections and opens access to poorly sampled Milky Way regions, yet chemical characterization of CCs in such regions remains scarce.
AI.method: The authors analyze 27 CCs with ERIS@VLT in J-band low-resolution mode (R~4000). They combine PySME with 1D MARCS atmosphere models and NLTE grids to simultaneously optimize atmospheric parameters via spectral fitting. The approach is validated against high-resolution optical studies and by re-analysis of archival optical spectra for targets in common.
AI.result: Good consistency is found in both metallicity and chemical abundances relative to optical references. Mean abundance ratios are [Mg/Fe] = 0.01 ± 0.12 dex and [Si/Fe] = 0.10 ± 0.09 dex, in agreement with reference samples. Mg and Si abundances are reported for the first time for 12 CCs. Two of the most distant Galactic CCs (R_GC ≈ 28–29 kpc; vertical heights ≈ +4.8 kpc and ≈ −5.3 kpc) show distinct kinematic properties, though more data are needed to constrain their nature.
AI.conclusion: Low-resolution J-band spectroscopy is a reliable diagnostic for chemical investigations in highly obscured Galactic regions that are inaccessible at optical wavelengths, extending the reach of Cepheid-based chemical and kinematic studies.

title: The kinematic response of RGB centroids and O--B stars to the Milky Way spiral structure: testing the solid-body rotation of the spiral pattern
summary: Using the centroid velocities of RGB stars and the individual velocities of O-B stars from the Gaia DR3, we test whether the spiral structure in the investigated region of the Galaxy can be described by a single wave with a constant pattern speed within the framework of Lin-Shu density-wave theory. The amplitudes of the radial and azimuthal velocity perturbations are determined for three centroid samples: centroids within strips 350 pc wide around five spiral arms; centroids within the same strips, with an additional condition on the radial gradient of the radial velocity, $M_{11}^+$; and all centroids within $5 \leq R \leq 15$ kpc and $130^\circ \leq θ\leq 270^\circ$. The periodic and smooth non-periodic velocity components are fitted simultaneously. For each sample, the amplitudes derived from the RGB centroid velocities and the individual O-B stellar velocities are used to calculate the relative frequency as a function of Galactocentric radius, $R$, and subsequently the pattern speed at different radii. The analysis is performed for both stellar populations and for two assumed numbers of spiral arms, $m=4$ and $m=5$, using either the amplitude ratio or the radial amplitude alone. None of the cases considered supports a constant pattern speed within the adopted Lin-Shu model. We regard the pattern speed inferred from the radial solution for a specified perturbing potential as our main result. The estimate based on the amplitude ratio provides a complementary result that is consistent with the main conclusion of a non-constant pattern speed, but is less reliable because of the azimuthal response.

AI.tldr: Using Gaia DR3 kinematics of RGB centroids and O-B stars, the authors show that no single constant pattern speed can describe the spiral structure in the studied Galactic region within the Lin-Shu density-wave model.
AI.motivation: Lin-Shu density-wave theory predicts spiral structure describable by a single wave with a constant pattern speed. The authors test this assumption directly against Gaia DR3 velocity data in a specific Galactic region.
AI.method: Centroid velocities of RGB stars and individual O-B star velocities from Gaia DR3. Three centroid samples: strips 350 pc wide around five spiral arms; same strips with an added condition on the radial gradient of radial velocity (M11+); and all centroids in 5 <= R <= 15 kpc, 130° <= θ <= 270°. Periodic and smooth non-periodic velocity components fitted simultaneously. For each sample, RGB and O-B amplitudes yield relative frequency as a function of Galactocentric radius R, and hence pattern speed at different radii, for two stellar populations and for m=4 and m=5, using either the amplitude ratio or the radial amplitude alone.
AI.result: None of the cases considered supports a constant pattern speed within the Lin-Shu model; the inferred pattern speed varies with Galactocentric radius.
AI.conclusion: The main result is the pattern speed inferred from the radial solution for a specified perturbing potential. The amplitude-ratio estimate is complementary and consistent with a non-constant pattern speed but less reliable due to azimuthal response.

title: All-sky spectroscopic survey of bright δ Scuti stars from TESS Projected rotational velocities and pulsation characteristics
summary: Context. The second most numerous class of pulsating stars -- $δ$ Scuti ($δ$ Sct) -- lack a homogeneous, large-scale spectroscopic sample in the Kepler and TESS era, limiting our understanding of how rotation shapes stellar pulsations. Aims. We analyse projected rotational velocities ($v \sin i$) from high-resolution spectroscopy alongside 2-minute TESS photometry to establish empirical links between stellar rotation and pulsation parameters. Methods. Combining observations from three high-resolution échelle spectrographs with two spectral libraries, we assemble an all-sky sample of 262 $δ$ Sct stars ($R = 25\,000$ to $115\,000$). We derive $v \sin i$ via three independent methods and extract pulsation frequencies and amplitudes from TESS light curves. Results. The $v \sin i$ distribution is unimodal, with a mean of $120.3\text{ km s}^{-1}$ and peak probability at $113.8\text{ km s}^{-1}$. Minimum ($ν_{\rm min}$), dominant ($ν_{\rm dom}$), amplitude-weighted ($ν_{\rm AW}$), and power-weighted ($ν_{\rm PW}$) frequencies decrease with $v \sin i / v_{\rm crit}$, whereas maximum frequency ($ν_{\rm max}$) does not. Fast rotators show a narrower range of photometric and pulsation amplitudes than slow rotators, and their lower mean stellar density ($\barρ$) cannot fully explain the frequency decrease. Calibrating Gaia's $v_{\rm broad}$ against our measurements removes its systematic offset, enabling use across larger $δ$ Sct samples. Multi-spectrum comparisons reveal method discrepancies mainly for fast rotators ($v \sin i > 200\text{ km s}^{-1}$) and inter-spectrograph offsets up to $20\text{ km s}^{-1}$. Conclusions. We present the largest homogeneous high-resolution $v \sin i$ sample for bright $δ$ Sct stars in the TESS era, showing that $v \sin i$ measurements in pulsating stars require careful treatment across instruments and velocity regimes.

AI.tldr: The authors build the largest homogeneous high-resolution v sin i sample (262 stars) of δ Scuti stars with 2-minute TESS photometry, showing that characteristic pulsation frequencies decrease with rotation ratio v sin i / v_crit and identifying instrumental and methodological caveats.
AI.motivation: δ Scuti stars are the second most numerous class of pulsators but lack a homogeneous, large-scale spectroscopic sample in the Kepler/TESS era, which limits understanding of how rotation shapes stellar pulsations.
AI.method: All-sky sample of 262 δ Sct stars from three high-resolution échelle spectrographs and two spectral libraries (R = 25,000–115,000). Projected rotational velocities derived via three independent methods; pulsation frequencies and amplitudes extracted from 2-minute TESS light curves. Gaia v_broad calibrated against the measurements.
AI.result: Unimodal v sin i distribution (mean 120.3 km/s, peak 113.8 km/s). Minimum, dominant, amplitude-weighted and power-weighted frequencies decrease with v sin i / v_crit, while maximum frequency does not. Fast rotators show narrower amplitude ranges, and lower mean density does not fully explain the frequency decrease. Gaia v_broad offset removed by calibration. Method discrepancies mainly for v sin i > 200 km/s, with inter-spectrograph offsets up to 20 km/s.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the largest homogeneous high-resolution v sin i sample for bright δ Sct stars in the TESS era and shows that v sin i measurements in pulsating stars require careful treatment across instruments and velocity regimes.

title: The Velocity Curves and Three-Dimensional Kinematics of the Milky Way from Gaia DR3
summary: We investigate the fundamental kinematic parameters of stellar motions in the Milky Way using a statistical sample of 27,485,720 stars with measured three-dimensional velocities from the Gaia DR3 catalogue. From these data, we determine the local solar velocity $(U_{\odot},V_{\odot},W_{\odot}) = \left(10.5\pm0.7,14.5\pm0.9,7.33\pm0.1\right) ~\mathrm{km/s}$, the average rotation velocity\linebreak $\mathrm{V}_{0} = \left( 228\pm4\right) $ km/s, and the circular velocity $\mathrm{V}_{c} = \left( 234\pm4\right) $ {km/s,} both at the radius $R_{\odot}$. Next, within the range of $3-14$ kpc, we derive the Galactic circular velocity curve $\mathrm{V}_{c}(R)$ and determine the average spherical components of the stellar velocities as functions of both Galactocentric radius $R$ and distance from the Galactic plane $\left\vert Z\right\vert $. Two-dimensional $R-Z$ maps of these components reveal a complex three-dimensional kinematic structure. In particular, the pattern observed at $R\lesssim5$ kpc can be associated with the influence of the Galactic bar. To facilitate the description of the observations, we employ a simplified axisymmetric Monte Carlo model with several free parameters that reproduces the main kinematic trends.

AI.tldr: Using ~27.5 million Gaia DR3 stars with 3D velocities, the authors measure the solar motion, rotation/circular velocities at R_⊙, derive V_c(R) over 3–14 kpc, and map the R–Z dependence of mean spherical velocity components, interpreting inner-Galaxy patterns as bar influence.
AI.motivation: Fundamental kinematic parameters of the Milky Way (solar motion, rotation and circular velocities, the rotation curve, and the spatial dependence of stellar mean motions) need precise, large-sample determination; Gaia DR3's vast 3D velocity catalogue enables this and allows mapping of non-axisymmetric structure such as the bar.
AI.method: Statistical analysis of 27,485,720 Gaia DR3 stars with measured three-dimensional velocities. Solar velocity components and V_0, V_c at R_⊙ are fitted; the circular velocity curve V_c(R) is derived over 3–14 kpc; average spherical velocity components are computed as functions of Galactocentric radius R and |Z|; two-dimensional R–Z maps are constructed. A simplified axisymmetric Monte Carlo model with several free parameters is used to reproduce the main trends.
AI.result: (U_⊙, V_⊙, W_⊙) = (10.5±0.7, 14.5±0.9, 7.33±0.1) km/s; average rotation velocity V_0 = 228±4 km/s and circular velocity V_c = 234±4 km/s at R_⊙; V_c(R) obtained for 3–14 kpc; R–Z maps reveal a complex three-dimensional kinematic structure, with the pattern at R ≲ 5 kpc attributable to the Galactic bar.
AI.conclusion: Large Gaia DR3 samples yield precise local kinematic parameters and a 3–14 kpc rotation curve, while R–Z maps expose non-axisymmetric, bar-driven kinematics in the inner Galaxy; a simple axisymmetric Monte Carlo model captures the dominant trends, providing a baseline against which more complex (e.g., barred) models can be compared.

title: Unexpected Plateau: The Constant $ \rm \log ε(Th/Eu)$ Ratio of Actinide-Boost Stars
summary: The astrophysical site of the rapid neutron-capture process ($r$-process) is still one of the major open questions in astronomy. A key mystery is the origin of the peculiar actinide-to-lanthanide ratio found in the so called actinide-boost stars, with $ \rm \log ε(Th/Eu)>-0.35$. Here we present the largest sample of Th measurements in stars formed in an external galaxy, Gaia Sausage Enceladus. From this sample, we present the three most metal-rich actinide-boost stars discovered to date, $\rm -1.6<[Fe/H]<-1.1$. In addition, we measured Th in a comparison sample of Milky Way stars formed in situ, and compiled Th measurements from the literature which do not account for non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) effects. After applying NLTE corrections to the combined sample, a bimodality in the $\rm\logε(Th/Eu)$ ratio is revealed. Unexpectedly, actinide-boost stars lie on a very narrow $(σ=0.02)$ plateau of $\rm \logε(Th/Eu)=-0.2$, clearly separated from actinide-normal stars. Most (if not all) of the actinide-boost stars in our sample originate from outside the Milky Way. Chemical evolution models show that such a plateau can arise, even at [Fe/H] = $-$1, when a single actinide-rich event dominates the r-process content of a small or gas-depleted system. Combined with other evidence, our results suggest that mergers with neutron stars are the most promising astrophysical site for actinide-boost stars.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the largest sample of Th abundances in Gaia Sausage Enceladus stars and, after NLTE corrections, reveals a narrow actinide-boost plateau at log ε(Th/Eu) = −0.2, arguing that neutron-star mergers are the most promising site for actinide-boost stars.
AI.motivation: The astrophysical site of the r-process remains a major open question, and the origin of the peculiar actinide-to-lanthanide ratio in actinide-boost stars (log ε(Th/Eu) > −0.35) is unexplained.
AI.method: Measure Th in the largest sample of stars formed in the external Gaia Sausage Enceladus galaxy, including the three most metal-rich actinide-boost stars known (−1.6 < [Fe/H] < −1.1); measure Th in an in-situ Milky Way comparison sample; compile literature Th measurements lacking NLTE treatment; apply NLTE corrections to the combined sample; and run chemical evolution models.
AI.result: NLTE-corrected data reveal bimodality in log ε(Th/Eu): actinide-boost stars form a narrow plateau (σ = 0.02) at log ε(Th/Eu) = −0.2, clearly separated from actinide-normal stars. Most (if not all) actinide-boost stars originate outside the Milky Way. Models show such a plateau can arise even at [Fe/H] = −1 when a single actinide-rich event dominates the r-process content of a small or gas-depleted system.
AI.conclusion: Combined with other evidence, mergers with neutron stars are the most promising astrophysical site for actinide-boost stars.

title: A COMPASS to the Galaxy: Joint nucleosynthetic yield set comparison and parameter inference in Galactic chemical evolution
summary: Galactic Chemical Evolution (GCE) models connect stellar nucleosynthesis to observed abundance patterns, but their interpretation requires simultaneous parameter inference and comparison between competing stellar yield prescriptions. This remains challenging due to intractable likelihoods and growing dataset complexity. Using compass, a novel simulation-based inference framework, we perform, for the first time, amortized joint Bayesian model comparison and parameter inference for GCE models with intractable likelihoods within a unified architecture. Compass employs a conditional score-based diffusion model with a transformer architecture to learn both the posterior and likelihood directly from forward simulations, enabling efficient inference and likelihood-based ranking of competing nucleosynthetic yield sets. In controlled tests, compass identifies the generating yield set and recovers ground-truth parameters with accuracy comparable to existing simulation-based inference (SBI) methods, while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude. Applied to Milky Way data, the framework favors a hybrid NuGrid + IllustrisTNG yield prescription, confirmed by an independent classifier, and infers an initial mass function slope of $α_{\rm IMF} = -2.65 \pm 0.02$ and a SN$_{\rm Ia}$ normalization of $\log(N_{\rm Ia}) = -2.81 \pm 0.02$, with a systematic spread of $\approx 0.3$ in $α_{\rm IMF}$ between the best-ranked yield sets, consistent with independent constraints. The attention mechanism confirms that the inferred parameters are driven by physically meaningful abundance signatures. By unifying amortized parameter inference, Bayesian model comparison, and interpretability in a single probabilistic framework, compass provides a scalable approach for precision chemical evolution studies with current and forthcoming spectroscopic surveys.

AI.tldr: Compass, a transformer-based conditional score-based diffusion SBI framework, performs amortized joint Bayesian model comparison and parameter inference for intractable-likelihood GCE models, ranking stellar yield sets at orders-of-magnitude lower cost and inferring Milky Way GCE parameters.
AI.motivation: GCE models link nucleosynthesis to observed abundances, but interpreting them requires simultaneous parameter inference and comparison among competing yield prescriptions—hampered by intractable likelihoods and growing data complexity.
AI.method: Compass uses a conditional score-based diffusion model with a transformer architecture to learn both posterior and likelihood directly from forward simulations, enabling efficient inference and likelihood-based ranking of yield sets; attention provides interpretability. Validated on controlled tests and applied to Milky Way data with an independent classifier cross-check.
AI.result: Recovers generating yield set and ground-truth parameters comparably to existing SBI at orders-of-magnitude lower cost. Milky Way data favor a hybrid NuGrid + IllustrisTNG prescription, yielding α_IMF = -2.65 ± 0.02 and log(N_Ia) = -2.81 ± 0.02, with ~0.3 systematic spread in α_IMF across top-ranked yield sets; attention confirms physically meaningful abundance drivers.
AI.conclusion: Unifying amortized inference, Bayesian model comparison, and interpretability in one probabilistic framework, compass offers a scalable route to precision chemical evolution studies with current and forthcoming spectroscopic surveys.

title: Two new Li-rich dwarf stars in M 4: abundance patterns and possible origins
summary: Context. Li-rich stars are rare, and only 16 are known in globular clusters (GCs), spanning evolutionary stages from the main sequence turnoff to the red giant branch. Their origin is still debated, but GCs provide a unique environment to discriminate among proposed mechanisms for Li enrichment. Aims. We aim to characterise two newly discovered Li-rich dwarf stars, 44606 and 58195, in the GC M 4 (NGC 6121) and investigate their origin among the formation channels proposed in the literature. The previously known Li-rich star in the cluster, namely 37934, was re-analyzed for comparison. Methods. We performed a standard abundance analysis based on 1D model atmospheres in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) on high-resolution Ultraviolet and Visual Echelle Spectrograph (UVES). We measured the projected rotational velocity and searched for chromospheric activity. Results. We derive A(Li)= 2.58, 2.51 dex for stars 44606 and 58195, respectively, significantly different from the A(Li) distribution of normal dwarfs in M 4. For the known Li-rich star 37934, we obtain A(Li)= 3.01 dex, consistent with previous work. We estimate detailed abundances of 24 species (Li, C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, S, K, Ca, Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Sr, Y, Zr, Ba, and Nd) in the three stars. None of our targets show detectable rotational broadening or chromospheric activity. Conclusions. The Li-rich stars analysed here are unevolved, ruling out in-situ Li production. Planet engulfment is very unlikely in GCs, and we detect no present-day rotation or activity. By exclusion, the most plausible remaining scenarios involve different types of interaction with a companion, including dynamical interactions, mass transfer, and mergers. Currently, we have not detected a companion.

AI.tldr: Two new Li-rich dwarf stars (44606, 58195) in the globular cluster M4 are confirmed with A(Li)=2.58 and 2.51 dex, plus a re-analysis of the known Li-rich star 37934 (A(Li)=3.01 dex); their unevolved nature and lack of rotation/activity point to companion-interaction scenarios for Li enrichment.

AI.method: High-resolution UVES spectroscopy with standard 1D LTE model-atmosphere abundance analysis; measurement of projected rotational velocity and search for chromospheric activity; detailed abundances of 24 species (Li, C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, S, K, Ca, Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Sr, Y, Zr, Ba, Nd) for stars 44606, 58195, and 37934.

title: On the origin of Milky Way binary black holes with LISA
summary: Primordial black holes (PBHs) may constitute a fraction of dark matter, but distinguishing them from black holes of stellar origin remains a major challenge. We propose a new method based on the three-dimensional localization of Galactic Binary Black Holes (BBHs) by the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). While stellar-origin BBHs are expected to be associated with the stellar distribution of the Milky Way, PBHs may trace its more extended dark matter halo. We introduce a spatial overlap ratio that compares the gravitational-wave localization of each binary with the normalized stellar and dark matter density profiles. Using a Fisher-matrix forecast and 1000 Monte Carlo realizations of a 10-year LISA mission, we find that detecting three BBHs with an overlap ratio ln B < 0 occurs in approximately 99% of simulations where BBHs trace dark matter, but in fewer than 0.1% of simulations where they follow the stellar distribution, even when including a stellar halo containing 3% of the Galactic stellar mass. These results suggest that the localization of only a few Galactic BBHs could provide strong evidence for a primordial population, offering an independent test of their possible contribution to dark matter.

AI.tldr: A spatial overlap ratio comparing LISA gravitational-wave localizations of Galactic binary black holes with stellar vs. dark matter density profiles can distinguish primordial from stellar-origin BBHs using only a few detections.
AI.motivation: Primordial black holes (PBHs) may contribute to dark matter, but distinguishing them from stellar-origin black holes is a major open challenge. Stellar-origin BBHs should trace the Milky Way stellar distribution, while PBHs may follow the more extended dark matter halo, offering a potential spatial discriminator.
AI.method: The authors introduce a spatial overlap ratio (ln B) that compares each binary's LISA three-dimensional gravitational-wave localization against normalized stellar and dark matter density profiles. They perform a Fisher-matrix forecast with 1000 Monte Carlo realizations of a 10-year LISA mission.
AI.result: Detecting three BBHs with overlap ratio ln B < 0 occurs in ~99% of simulations where BBHs trace dark matter, but in <0.1% of simulations where they follow the stellar distribution, even including a stellar halo containing 3% of the Galactic stellar mass.
AI.conclusion: Localizing only a few Galactic BBHs could provide strong evidence for a primordial population, yielding an independent test of their possible contribution to dark matter.

title: OGHReS: Discovery of a giant hub-filament system at the edge of the Galactic molecular disc
summary: We present the discovery and characterisation of G195.65$-$0.10 (also known as the $λ$-complex), a giant hub-filament system identified by the Outer Galaxy High Resolution Survey (OGHReS). The complex contains 61 spatially and kinematically coherent HiGAL clumps with a mean velocity of $V_{\rm LSR}=32.85$ km/s and a velocity dispersion between clumps of 1.97 km/s. A $Gaia$ parallax measurement of the central emission-line star MWC 137 associated with an embedded cluster gives a heliocentric distance of 5.2$^{+0.8}_{-0.6}$ kpc, placing the complex at a Galactocentric radius of 13.2 kpc. The molecular structure spans approximately $35\times63$ pc and contains $\sim 1.6\times10^{5}$ M$_\odot$ of molecular gas, including $\sim 5 \times 10^{4}$ M$_\odot$ in dense clumps. The molecular emission is organised into three prominent velocity-coherent filaments that converge on a dense central hub. Of the associated clumps, 16 are protostellar and 45 are gravitationally bound but currently starless. The protostellar clumps are significantly more concentrated towards the hub than the starless population, with median projected offsets of 6.65 and 15.83 pc, respectively. Moreover, the luminosity-to-mass ratio of the protostellar clumps decreases significantly with increasing distance from the hub, indicating that the most evolutionarily advanced sources are preferentially located in the central region. These results reveal a systematic concentration of dense gas and increasingly evolved star formation towards the hub, with organised large-scale gas motions throughout the filamentary network. The $λ$-complex therefore provides an unprecedented laboratory to understand hierarchical and high-mass star formation in the outer Galactic disc.

AI.tldr: The paper discovers and characterises G195.65−0.10 (the λ-complex), a giant hub-filament system in the outer Galactic disc at 13.2 kpc Galactocentric radius, revealing systematic concentration of dense gas and increasingly evolved star formation toward a central hub.
AI.motivation: Understanding hierarchical and high-mass star formation in the outer Galactic disc lacks well-characterised, spatially resolved laboratories where large-scale gas motions, dense clump populations, and star formation activity can be studied together.
AI.method: Identify the complex via the Outer Galaxy High Resolution Survey (OGHReS); catalogue 61 spatially and kinematically coherent HiGAL clumps (V_LSR ≈ 32.85 km/s, inter-clump velocity dispersion 1.97 km/s); derive distance from a Gaia parallax of the central emission-line star MWC 137; analyse molecular structure, filament kinematics, and clump properties (protostellar vs. starless, offsets, luminosity-to-mass ratios).
AI.result: The complex lies at 5.2(+0.8/−0.6) kpc heliocentric distance (13.2 kpc Galactocentric), spans ~35×63 pc with ~1.6×10^5 M⊙ of molecular gas (~5×10^4 M⊙ in dense clumps), organised into three velocity-coherent filaments converging on a dense central hub. Of 61 clumps, 16 are protostellar and 45 are gravitationally bound but starless; protostellar clumps are more centrally concentrated (median projected offset 6.65 vs. 15.83 pc) and their luminosity-to-mass ratio decreases with distance from the hub.
AI.conclusion: The λ-complex shows a systematic concentration of dense gas and progressively evolved star formation toward the hub, with organised large-scale gas motions throughout the filamentary network, providing an exceptional laboratory for studying hierarchical and high-mass star formation in the outer Galactic disc.

title: Kinetic Monte Carlo modeling of ammonium formate NH$_4^+$HCOO$^-$ and ammonium cyanate NH$_4^+$OCN$^-$ in interstellar ices
summary: JWST observations have revealed evidence for NH$_4^+$ in the ices of the Chamaeleon I dark molecular cloud, with HCOO$^-$ and OCN$^-$ likely counter ions. Laboratory experiments have demonstrated that ammonium formate and ammonium cyanate can form through acid-base reactions involving NH$_3$ at cryogenic temperatures. The formation of these two ammonium salts are simulated to investigate their formation in dark-cloud ices and assess their sensitivity to uncertainties in the chemical reaction network, including the recently considered HOCO-mediated pathway for CO$_2$ formation, as well as variations in the cosmic-ray ionization rate, cloud collapse timescale and density, and elemental depletion. Our modeling framework consists of microscopic kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) simulations of grain-surface chemistry augmented by UCLCHEM gas-phase and physical cloud evolution simulations. The microscopic KMC method provides for explicit simulation of the location, movement and reaction of ice species, making it particularly well-suited to model acid-base chemistry of NH$_4^+$-salt formation, occurring within the ice mantle over extended timescales. The simulations produce the canonical ice-evolution sequence, with an initially H$_2$O-rich ice followed by a layer dominated by CO and CO$_2$. Salt production is dominated by NH$_4^+$HCOO$^-$, which is found to form predominantly during the H$_2$O-rich stage as its production is limited by the availability of NH$_3$. NH$_4^+$OCN$^-$ is found to form later at the interface between the H$_2$O- and CO-rich ice when the formation of its precursor acid HNCO is enabled. Despite the variations explored, the total NH$_4^+$ abundance, particularly relative to H$_2$O, remains remarkably robust and consistent with the observed abundance. Depending on the variation, a redistribution between counterions HCOO$^-$ and OCN$^-$ is observed.

AI.tldr: Microscopic kinetic Monte Carlo grain-surface chemistry simulations, coupled with UCLCHEM gas-phase and cloud-evolution models, reproduce the formation and observed abundance of ammonium salts (NH4+HCOO- and NH4+OCN-) in Chamaeleon I dark-cloud ices, with total NH4+ abundance robust against a wide range of physical and chemical uncertainties.
AI.motivation: JWST detection of NH4+ (with HCOO- and OCN- as likely counterions) in Chamaeleon I ices, plus laboratory evidence that ammonium formate and ammonium cyanate form via low-temperature acid-base reactions with NH3, motivates modeling how these salts form in dark-cloud ices and how sensitive their abundances are to uncertainties in the reaction network (e.g., HOCO-mediated CO2 pathway) and physical parameters.
AI.method: A hybrid framework combining microscopic kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) simulations of grain-surface chemistry with UCLCHEM gas-phase and physical cloud-evolution simulations. The KMC explicitly tracks the location, movement, and reaction of ice species, enabling modeling of acid-base salt formation within the ice mantle over long timescales. Parameter variations explored include the HOCO-mediated CO2 pathway, cosmic-ray ionization rate, cloud collapse timescale and density, and elemental depletion.
AI.result: Simulations reproduce the canonical ice-evolution sequence: an initially H2O-rich ice followed by a CO/CO2-dominated layer. NH4+HCOO- dominates salt production, forming mainly during the H2O-rich stage and limited by NH3 availability. NH4+OCN- forms later at the interface between H2O- and CO-rich ice, once precursor HNCO is enabled. Total NH4+ abundance, especially relative to H2O, remains remarkably robust and consistent with JWST observations; parameter variations mainly redistribute abundance between HCOO- and OCN- counterions.
AI.conclusion: The KMC/UCLCHEM framework successfully captures NH4+-salt formation chemistry in dark-cloud ices. The NH4+ abundance is insensitive to the explored chemical and physical uncertainties and matches observations, while the counterion balance is more sensitive; this supports the salt interpretation of JWST ice spectra and highlights the value of microscopic KMC for modeling acid-base ice chemistry.

title: Gravitational Waves from Population III Black Hole Mergers in Primordial Gas Disks: Constraining Astrophysical Scenarios with the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna and the Einstein Telescope
summary: The first generation of metal-free Population III (Pop~III) stars provides a possible formation channel for the black hole (BH) seeds in the early Universe. Their remnants may grow through gas accretion and mergers, producing gravitational wave (GW) signals detectable by future observatories. We develop a semi-analytical model of fragmentation in a primordial self-gravitating gas disk within minihaloes at $z > 15$, motivated by high-resolution cosmological simulations. The resulting Pop~III stars form around a central primary, some leaving massive BH remnants that migrate towards the central BH through dynamical friction from gas and dark matter, while the central BH grows through accretion and mergers. For a $10^6~{\rm M_\odot}$ halo at $z=20$, we explore how the initial mass function (IMF) and BH accretion efficiency affect detectability with the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) and the Einstein Telescope (ET). We find that both detectors can potentially reveal mergers of Pop III remnant BHs, but favor different astrophysical conditions. LISA pinpoints more massive central BHs ($\sim10^3$-$10^4 {\rm M_\odot}$), grown rapidly through mutual mergers alongside efficient gas accretion ($f_{\rm Edd}=1$), and a relatively top-heavy IMF ($α=0.8$). In contrast, detectability with ET favors lower-mass BHs, with less efficient accretion ($f_{\rm Edd}=0.01$) and a steeper IMF ($α=1.5$). These results highlight the potential of LISA and ET to probe Pop~III BH formation, growth, and mergers across different regions of parameter spaces, jointly constraining Pop~III star formation and early BH seed evolution.

AI.tldr: A semi-analytical model of Pop III star fragmentation in primordial disks (z > 15) shows that LISA and ET can detect remnant BH mergers under different conditions: LISA favors massive central BHs (~10^3–10^4 M☉) with efficient accretion and top-heavy IMF, while ET favors lower-mass BHs with weak accretion and steeper IMF.
AI.motivation: Metal-free Population III stars offer a possible formation channel for early-Universe BH seeds, whose growth via accretion and mergers may produce detectable gravitational waves; the paper aims to connect Pop III star formation parameters to the GW detectability of their remnant BHs.
AI.method: A semi-analytical model of fragmentation in a primordial self-gravitating gas disk within minihaloes at z > 15, motivated by high-resolution cosmological simulations. Pop III stars form around a central primary; some leave massive BH remnants that migrate inward via dynamical friction from gas and dark matter, while the central BH grows through accretion and mergers. For a 10^6 M☉ halo at z = 20, the IMF and BH accretion efficiency are varied to assess detectability with LISA and ET.

LISA detects more massive central BHs (~10^3–10^4 M☉) grown rapidly via mergers with efficient accretion (f_Edd = 1) and a top-heavy IMF (α = 0.8). ET favors lower-mass BHs, less efficient accretion (f_Edd = 0.01), and a steeper IMF (α = 1.5).
AI.conclusion: LISA and ET probe complementary regions of parameter space for Pop III BH formation, growth, and mergers, jointly constraining Pop III star formation and early BH seed evolution.
